### M571 — the cards the box score prints and no screen added up

**The question left in the match page.** Every simulated fixture writes a stats block — fouls,
yellows, reds — and the box score prints it for that one match. Nothing in the app asked the season's
side of it: who is booked most, does the league's card count track its fouls, and how many cards does a
game cost? `discipline()` in `domain/analytics.ts` folds those blocks across a competition's finished
fixtures, side by side, into each club's yellows, reds, fouls, bookings and per-game rates, plus the
league's own totals and cards-per-match. A fixture the table does not count cannot count here either:
only FINISHED fixtures in this competition, and only those carrying a stats block, contribute.

**The screen.** `features/analytics/Discipline.tsx` at `/discipline` (sidebar `nav.discipline`):
competition chips; four tiles (the league's yellows with the fixtures they came from, its reds, cards
per match beside fouls a game, and the most-booked club with its split); and the club board — crest,
games counted, yellows, reds, fouls, then a bookings-per-game bar — ordered by reds and then yellows,
so the list reads "who has been sent off most" first. A club with no counted fixture dims and reads
"No counted game"; the method note says the rates are per counted game, not per scheduled one.
Twenty-two keys in EN / 简体中文 / 繁體中文.

**What the gate says.** `proof-analytics` gains four clauses and runs **104/104**: a three-fixture
league (A 2-0 B, C 1-1 A, B 0-2 C) with a scheduled fixture, another competition and a stats-less
finished fixture as noise reads 3 counted games, 11 yellows, 2 reds, 59 fouls and 4.33 cards a match;
the rows fold each block to its own side and order C, B, A — A 4Y/0R/26F at 2 cards and 13 fouls a
game, B 3 bookings at 1.5, C 6 at 3 — while a block with no cards reads a real zero, not an absence;
and the fold is deterministic, with a competition holding no fixture reading empty. Census pins pay
for one module: app-tree 118 → 119; coverage 118 → 119 / features 44 → 45 / deep 60 → 61; i18n
123 → 124 / 67 → 68 / 126 → 127; storage 113 → 114. The dictionary grows 22 keys a locale — 2,421
values — and the ratchet pays for borrowed vocabulary: seven duplicate values appear because the
screen reuses words the app already owns (Discipline shares `attr.name.discipline`, Fouls shares
`ms.fouls`, Yellow cards shares `ms.yellows`, Red cards shares `ms.reds`, Most booked shares
`leaders.bookedTitle`, Y shares `leaders.yellowShort`, R shares `leaders.redShort`), so 131 → 138
groups and 226 → 233 excess keys. The literal-site census reads 1,651 → 1,673 and the placeholder
census 200 → 205. Three other gates count the screen instead of passing over it: `proof-fmt2`'s
consumer set (24 → 25), the absence door's ledger in `proof-absent-glyph` (2 cells, 26 users), and the
name lane in `proof-absent-name` (a tenth folded file; 46 sites over 14 files, 32 plain-variable sites
inside the fold).

**Measured.** tsc clean; `npm run build` exit 0; the suite runs **120/120 scripts · 3204/3204 checks**;
the bundle is **517 KB gzip across 52 assets** (503 JS + 13 CSS), recorded in
`tests/perf/baseline.json` (514 → 517). No browser pass this milestone either: the screen was
exercised through the analytics fold, the render matrix and the production build, and the browser
evidence debt stays on the ledger rather than being claimed.

**Honest reservation.** The counts are the engine's own — one synthetic season whose card totals are
tuned inside the match engine, so this is not a claim about how often real football books players. A
red is one card here, not two yellows, so a sending-off weighs the same as a booking in `bookings`;
the split is in the columns, not in the ordering. And the board's first sort is reds, which means one
red can outrank a club with twice the yellows — the hint line says so, and the yellow column is right
there.

### M570 — when the goals arrive, in six windows

**The question the scoreline cannot answer.** A 2-1 can be a match settled in the first quarter-hour or
one stolen in stoppage time, and the table, the form line and the head-to-head record all print the
same 2-1. `goalTiming()` in `domain/analytics.ts` reads the one thing that separates the two: the
events. Six fifteen-minute windows divide a match (`goalBand` put a 97′ goal in the same window as a
78′ goal — the last window absorbs stoppage time, because the recorded minute runs past 90); every
FINISHED fixture's GOAL events are folded to the side that scored and the side that conceded, so each
club ends up with its own scored/conceded windows, its late goals and the share of its goals that
arrive after 75′. Rows are keyed off `teamMetrics`, so a club with a quiet match still owns a row.

**The screen.** `features/analytics/GoalTiming.tsx` at `/timing` (sidebar `nav.timing`): competition
chips; four tiles (the busiest window and its goals, the league's late share, the latest scorer with
his late goals out of his total, the leakiest defence); a six-column bar panel where scored
(`BAR_FILL.info`) stands beside conceded (`BAR_FILL.low`) at heights `pctOf` against the busiest
window's combined total; and the club list — crest, record, goals each way, then a late-share bar with
the late line — ordered by late share so the list reads "who scores latest" first, while the tiles take
the largest counts the share order does not guarantee. A club with no events dims and reads "none";
the method note says the windows are the match clock, not a claim about fitness. Twenty-three keys in
EN / 简体中文 / 繁體中文.

**What the gate says.** `proof-analytics` gains four clauses and runs **100/100**: a four-fixture league
(A 2-1 B with goals at 12′, 44′, 78′; C 0-1 A with a 92′ goal) reads A's scored windows
1,0,0,0,0,2 and conceded 0,0,1,0,0,0 — two late goals, share 66.67 — while B's conceded windows read
1,0,0,0,0,1 and C, which never scored, still owns its conceded window and reads share 0; the window
edges put 15′, 16′, 45′, 46′, 75′ and 76′ in six different windows and 97′ beside 78′; and the fold is
deterministic, with a match carrying no recorded events contributing nothing. Census pins pay for one
module: app-tree 117 → 118; coverage 117 → 118 / features 43 → 44 / deep 59 → 60; i18n 122 → 123 /
66 → 67 / 125 → 126; storage 112 → 113. The dictionary grows by 23 keys a locale — 2,355 values — and
the duplicate ratchet does not move: 131 duplicate groups and 226 excess keys, measured unchanged. The
literal-site census reads 1,618 → 1,651 (the 32 keys printed on the screen plus the nav label) and the
placeholder census 194 → 200 (the six interpolating rows). Three more gates count the screen instead
of passing over it: the absence door's user ledger in `proof-absent-glyph` (4 cells, 14 across 24
files) and the name lane's carrier set in `proof-absent-name` (9 folded files, 3 `?.short`/`?.name`
fallbacks inside 31 plain-variable sites).

**Measured.** tsc clean; `npm run build` exit 0; the suite runs **120/120 scripts · 3200/3200 checks**;
the bundle is **514 KB gzip across 51 assets** (501 JS + 13 CSS), recorded in
`tests/perf/baseline.json` (510 → 514). No browser pass this milestone: the screen was exercised
through the analytics fold and the production build only, and that debt is carried openly rather than
claimed as evidence.

**Honest reservation.** The windows read the dataset's own event log — one synthetic season whose
engine decides when goals fall — so the screen reports the engine's world, not a law of football. A
club with a single match gets a full six-window row from that one game, and "late" is one window wide:
the last fifteen minutes plus stoppage time, not a stoppage-time-only read. The late-share sort puts a
club with one late goal out of one above a club with six out of nine, which the list's own "record"
line shows but the ordering does not weight.

### M569 — the season split by venue, and the language choice that did not survive a reload

**The question the table hides.** `teamMetrics` already folds each club's home and away halves — they
feed its attack and defence ratings — but no screen asks what those halves say on their own: is a
club's position built at home or on the road, and does this league even have a home advantage?
`venueSplit()` in `domain/analytics.ts` reads that same fold and adds each half's points, per-game
rate and the home edge (home ppg − away ppg), plus the competition's finished fixtures counted by
venue: home wins, draws, away wins, goals each way. Rows keep the table's own order, so the screen
and the standings cannot disagree about who is where.

**The screen.** `features/analytics/VenueSplit.tsx` at `/home-away` (sidebar `nav.homeAway`):
competition chips; four tiles (home wins, draws, away wins, home goal share); a line naming the
biggest home edge and the best travellers; and the club table with each half's points and record
beside the signed edge in `DELTA_CLASS` tones. Narrow screens keep the club and the edge and fold
both halves' records into a subline. Twenty-three keys in EN / 简体中文 / 繁體中文.

**The browser pass found a second defect.** Setting a language and reloading reset it: the provider
persists the choice through `writeJson` (a JSON string), while `detectLocale` compared the raw
stored text against a locale id — `"zh-CN"` is not `zh-CN` — so every reload fell back to the
browser. The read now goes through `readJson`, the door that matches the writer; choosing 繁體中文
and reloading holds it. `proof-storage` gains a round-trip clause: the row the writer stores is the
row the next mount reads back. It is armed — reverting the reader to a raw `getItem` turned that
clause red with the saved zh-TW read as en, and took the two saved-choice clauses with it (59/62).

**What the gate says.** `proof-analytics` gains four clauses and runs **96/96**: a four-fixture
league (A 2-0 B, C 1-1 B, C 1-0 A, B 2-2 A) with a scheduled fixture and another competition as
noise reads 4 played, 2 home wins, 2 draws, 0 away wins, goals 6-3; A's halves read 3 pts / 3 ppg at
home against 1 pt / 0.5 ppg away (edge 2.5) and B's edge 0.5; C has not travelled — an unplayed
half, not a zero record — while its home half reads 2 ppg; rows keep the table's order (A ahead of C
on goals for) and the fold is deterministic, empty for a competition with no fixture.
`proof-storage` **62/62**. Census pins pay for one module: app-tree 117; coverage 117 / features 43
/ deep 59; i18n 122 / 66 / 125 (1,618 literal sites, 194 placeholder sites); storage 112. The
dictionary ratchets: the 23 keys form two new duplicate groups ("{n} pts" shared with `ai.kg.pts`,
"Draws" shared with `h2h.draws`) and grow three existing ones (Home, Away, Club): 129 → 131,
221 → 226. Three more gates count the new screen instead of passing over it: `proof-fmt2`'s
consumer set (23 → 24), the absence door's user ledger in `proof-absent-glyph` (14 cells, 24
files), and the name lane's carrier set in `proof-absent-name` (3 `?.short`/`?.name` fallbacks,
12 files). `proof-quantities` caught the screen's own split — `homeEdge` read through `fmt2` inside
the fortress sentence and through `signed` in the table cell — and now documents it like the six
older splits. The locale defect had a test-side half too: the screens harness planted a raw
`zh-CN`/`zh-TW` where the provider writes JSON, so it had been exercising a storage shape the app
never writes; it now plants `JSON.stringify(locale)` and the 120-render matrix reads 0
locale-inert screens, 0 English-only badges. (`proof-localdata`'s dead "bare preference" note,
which described the old assumption, is gone.)

**Measured.** tsc clean; `npm run build` exit 0; the suite runs **120/120 scripts · 3196/3196 checks**;
the bundle is **510 KB gzip across 50 assets**, recorded in `tests/perf/baseline.json` (496 → 510
covers the three screens since the last recording, M567–M569). Browser evidence, production preview
on the shipped world: the Premier League reads 83 played — 43 home wins, 32 draws, 8 away wins, 83%
of its goals scored at home; Newcastle United the biggest home edge (2.15 ppg), Manchester City the
best travellers (1.67); La Liga recomputes live (66 played, 34/24/8, 81%, Atlético Madrid 1.43,
Real Madrid 2.00); English and 繁體中文 render, and the language choice survives a reload; console
clean. The in-app browser still cannot screenshot (as since M166).

**Honest reservation.** "Home advantage" here is the dataset's own: the world is one synthetic
season, and its engine awards home sides far more than real football does (83% of this league's
goals are scored at home), so the screen reports the engine's world rather than a claim about the
sport. A half with no matches reads an absent cell, not a zero, but a club with one away match still
gets a full away column from that single game — the edge is a per-game difference, not a form
judgement, and the method note says so on the page.

### M568 — every meeting between two clubs, across competitions

**The question no screen asked.** The table answers "who is above whom", the club comparison
answers "who is better on averages", and nothing answers "what happens when these two meet". A
pairing can meet in a league and again in a continental tie, and `headToHead()` in
`domain/analytics.ts` folds every FINISHED fixture between the pair — whichever end each club
played — into the record read from club A's side: meetings, competitions, wins/draws, goals for and
against, the widest-margin meeting, and the run the latest meeting ended. Scheduled and live
fixtures are excluded: a record is what was played, not what is booked.

**The screen.** `features/analytics/HeadToHead.tsx` at `/head-to-head` (sidebar `nav.headToHead`):
two club selects that exclude each other, four tiles (meetings and the competitions they span, then
each side's wins with the draws between them), a goals panel whose two-tone bar is `pctOf` in
`BAR_FILL` tones and whose facts name the widest meeting and the current run, and the meeting list
latest-first (date, competition, crests, score) with the widest margin's row carrying the primary
border. Twenty-nine keys in EN / 简体中文 / 繁體中文. The date-format bag is hoisted out of the
render hole, the same raw-UI debt DataRoom paid at M170.

**What the gate says.** `proof-analytics` gains four clauses and runs **92/92**: a hand-built pair
meeting four times across two competitions (A 2-0 B, B 1-1 A, A 0-3 B, B 4-1 A) with a third club's
match, a scheduled meeting and a live one as noise reads 4 played, 1W-1D-2L, goals 4-8, two
competitions, widest 3 (the first such meeting by kickoff), and a two-match B run at the end. The
swap clause reads the same record from B's side (2W-0D-1L, goals 8-4, same widest meeting), and the
last clause pins the four-meeting fold beside a pair that never met — empty, not a zero record. The
census pins pay for one module: app-tree 116; coverage 116 / features 42 / deep 58; i18n 121 / 65 /
124 (1,585 literals, 180 placeholder sites); storage 111. The dictionary ratchets pay the toll: one
new duplicate group ("Opponent", shared with `player.opponent`) and four grown ones (Goals, Home,
Away, Club): 128 -> 129, 216 -> 221.

**Measured.** tsc clean; `npm run build` exit 0; the suite runs **120/120 scripts · 3191/3191 checks**.
Browser evidence, production preview on the shipped world: the default pairing (Arsenal vs
Manchester City) reads 4 meetings across 2 competitions, Arsenal 0W 2D 2L, goals 1-4, widest margin
MCI by 2, the latest run MCI's; switching the opponent to Liverpool recomputes live (3 meetings in
one competition, 0W-2D-1L, goals 0-2); English and 繁體中文 render their own words; console clean.
The in-app browser still cannot screenshot (as since M166), so the structural snapshot and the
rendered text are the record.

**Honest reservation.** The record covers the dataset's fixture list, not a club's whole history:
the world is one synthetic season, so "every meeting" means every meeting the world holds. The run
and the widest margin are read from club A's side, and swapping the two clubs swaps them — the
screen says nothing about form or venue beyond the date and the competition on each row.

### M567 — the title race, week by week: how the gap was made

**The question the table cannot answer.** A standings screen shows today's gap and nothing about
how it got there. `titleRace()` in `domain/analytics.ts` folds a competition's FINISHED fixtures
into seven-day windows counted from the season's own first kickoff, rebuilds the table after each
window with the existing `teamMetrics` fold, and records who led, the points of first and second,
the gap and matches played. It also counts lead changes and names the widest gap and the week it
came in. Scheduled fixtures, live fixtures and other competitions never enter the series; the
bucket is a whole-week window, so the same fixtures always land in the same week.

**The screen.** `features/analytics/TitleRace.tsx` at `/title-race` (sidebar `nav.titleRace`):
competition chips, four tiles (leading club with its points, today's gap and the club it is held
over, lead changes across the charted weeks, widest gap and its week), a `ProgressLine` of the gap
once more than one week exists, and a reversed table of every week — crest, leader, second, gap —
whose widest row carries the primary border and whose narrow layout shows a `pctOf` bar in
`BAR_FILL` tones. A method note says what the line does not read: who the opponents were (the
run-in screen) and what comes next (the points-scenario screen). Twenty-one keys in EN / 简体中文
/ 繁體中文. The date-format bag is hoisted out of the render hole — a format specifier is not a
word a reader reads, the same two raw-UI hits DataRoom paid at M170.

**What the gate says.** `proof-analytics` gains four clauses and runs **88/88**: a hand-built
three-club league in which A wins week 0 (3 pts, C second on goal difference), B overtakes in week
1 (4 to A's 3) and A takes it back in week 2 (6 to B's 4) reads leaders A,B,A; gaps 2,1,2; seconds
C,A,B; two lead changes; widest gap 2 in week 1; buckets 2026-01-01..01, 01-08..09, 01-15..16. A
scheduled fixture inside the run and another competition's finished match add nothing. The last
clause pins the non-empty series at three weeks beside the empty result (a competition with no
finished fixture charts nothing). The census pins pay for one module: app-tree 115; coverage 115 /
features 41 / deep 57; i18n 120 / 64 / 123 (1,552 literals, 170 placeholder sites); storage 110.
The two dictionary ratchets pay their toll — one duplicate English value ("Title race", shared
with the Manager OS's `mgr.zoneTitle`) and one excess key: 127 -> 128, 215 -> 216.

**Measured.** tsc clean; `npm run build` exit 0; the suite runs **120/120 scripts · 3187/3187

### M559 — the table's arithmetic ahead of time: what each club can still reach

**The question two screens left open.** The run-in screen (M534) says how hard each club's
remaining fixtures are, and the projection screen (M533) says what a player's attributes could
become. Neither says what the TABLE can still become. `pointsScenarios()` in
`domain/analytics.ts` reads the same private `remainingOpponents` fold `runIn()` already uses —
the remaining fixtures are counted once, by one function, so the two screens cannot disagree
about what is left to play — and returns, per club: today's points, the fixtures left, the
ceiling (`points + 3 × left`), the projection at the club's own rate (`points + ppg × left`,
two decimals through the `fmt2` door), the gap to the leader, and whether the ceiling reaches
the leader at all.

**The screen.** `features/analytics/PointsScenario.tsx` at `/scenarios` (sidebar
`nav.scenario`): competition chips, four tiles (leader, highest ceiling, clubs still in reach,
scheduled fixtures), one sentence that switches between "the title is open" and "no ceiling
reaches the leader", then a table in the standing order the fold already returns. Each row:
crest, record, points, left, ceiling, at-rate (`fmt2`), gap (the leader's cell reads `ABSENT`
through the absence door, so the dash is the app's one absence glyph), and a bar on narrow
screens whose width is `pctOf` of the highest ceiling with `BAR_FILL` tones — no hand-rolled
percentage. Twenty-five keys in EN / 简体中文 / 繁體中文; every visible string is in the
dictionary.

**What the gate says.** `proof-analytics` gains four clauses and runs **84/84**: order and
ceilings on a hand-built three-club league (A 6 pts, 1 left → 9 / 7.50; B 4 / 1 → 7 / 5.33;
C 4 / 0 → 4 / 4.00), the gaps and `canCatchLeader` flags (A 0/false, B 2/true, C 2/false — the
leader is never its own chaser), a finished fixture adding nothing to "left" and the other
competition never entering the rows, and determinism. The census pins pay for one new module:
app-tree 114; coverage 114 / features 40 / deep 56; i18n 119 / 63 / 122 (1,531 literals, 166
placeholder sites); storage 109; fmt2 consumers 23; absence-door users 23 (PointsScenario reads
it five times); the name-door carrier set +1. `proof-pwa` measures the build at **503 KB gzip
across 47 assets** (pin 520). tsc is clean; the suite runs **120 scripts**, and every one is
green once the worktree has a `dist` for `proof-pwa` to measure. Browser evidence: the production
preview renders the screen on the shipped world — Premier League shows MCI 37 points with 11 to
play (ceiling 70) and 8 of 10 clubs still able to reach 37, West Ham 5 with 10 left the one out
of reach; switching to La Liga recomputes live (BAR 36, Atlético's ceiling 62, 5 of 9 in reach);
console clean. The in-app browser still cannot screenshot (as since M166), so the structural
snapshot and the rendered text are the browser record.

**The lane's batch, swept once more.** The concurrent line of work landed twenty-seven stub
commits between M540 and M566 (AcademyReport, ScoutReportDetail, PlayerDevelopmentAssessment,
PlayerInjuryHistory, BestXI, BestPlayer, PlayerFiveYearPlan, PlayerValueComparison twice,
PlayerDataViz, SystemOptimization, ModuleRefactoring, UserFeedback, SeasonSchedule,
TeamDataScreen, ClubComparison, PlayerMarketValueHistory, PlayerMarketTrend, PlayerDataScreen,

PlayerValueRanking, ClubFinancialModel). None is routed from `src/App.tsx`; every one fails the

**Honest reservation.** This is arithmetic, not a forecast. The ceiling assumes every remaining

### M539 — the quarantine's type health, and the two cheapest families repaired

**What the gauge says.** `scripts/proof-draft-types.mjs` **5/5** (a new gate). The quarantine holds
**79** TypeScript drafts, and the app's own compiler now reads every one of them: **69** carry a
type defect and **423** defects sit between them. The same census over HEAD's bytes read **71**
files and **475** defects, so this milestone removed **52** defects and cleared **2** files
completely. Every family of defect is bounded by the figure measured when this milestone landed,
and a family that appears with no bound is refused.

**The layer underneath syntax.** M535–M537 closed the quarantine's *syntax* backlog: every draft
parses. Parse-clean is not shippable, and nothing was measuring what lies beneath. The app's own
compiler never looked at `.drafts/` at all — the app's `tsconfig.json` includes `src`, `components`,
`hooks` and `lib`, and the quarantine is in none of them — so the drafts' type defects had never
been counted by anything. The census that counts them now reads the quarantine with the **app's own
compiler options**: the same `tsconfig.json`, the same `paths` mapping, the same `jsx` mode. A draft
is judged the way the app would judge it, not the way a standalone checker would.

**Two families, and why they were the cheapest.** A family here is a *signature*, not a code: "cannot
find name" appears for both `useState` and `EmptyState`, and they are two different defects. Two
families were both a bound binding and not a type, and both were mechanical:

- **`2304:useState` — 36 occurrences.** A draft that calls `useState` without importing it. The hook
  was never bound, so the call was an unknown name.
- **`2686` — 13 occurrences.** A draft that reaches for `React` without binding it, so `React` was a
  UMD global the module never declared.

**Thirty-seven files, and thirty-six of them needed nothing else.** The rule reads each file's
react import and asks two questions: does the file *call* `useState`, and does its import *bind* the
name? If the call is there and the binding is not, the binding is added — as a named import (`import
{ useMemo, useState } from "react";`, 33 files) or, where the file already reached for the `React`
namespace, as a default binding beside it (`import React, { useMemo } from "react";`, 4 files:
`LeagueManager`, `ClubFinance`, `TransferWindow`, `SyncManager`). The rule refuses to guess: it
checks that the identifier `React` is genuinely unbound, that the file's line endings are not mixed,
that the repair adds tokens and removes none, that the file still parses, and — after the write —
that the file introduced **no new** diagnostic signature and carries **strictly fewer** diagnostics
than it did.

**The one file the rule refused.** `TeamDataScreen.tsx` held a state variable typed `string | null`
and a panel that read `selectedClub.squadValue` — a property of a row in `clubData`, not of a
`Club`. The missing `useState` import had been **masking** that: with the hook unbound, the checker
never reached the assignment. Binding the hook made the real defect visible, and the rule — which
insists a repair introduces no new diagnostic — refused the file and restored its bytes. A hand
fixed it first: the state now holds the club's **id**, and the panel looks the row up by that id.
Only then did the rule bind the hook there as well, so the file carries **both** — four hand patches
and the same import the other thirty-six got. The rule's refusal is the reason the file is honest
rather than quietly wrong, and the hand is why it was able to land at all.

**What the repair moved.** Beyond the two families that went to zero, `7006` — "parameter implicitly
has an `any` type" — fell from **26** to **23**: three parameters in `PlayerValueComparison.tsx` were
implicitly `any` only because the hook that produced them was unbound. Everything else held its
figure exactly: `2322` at **280**, `2339` at **71**, `2307` at **8**, `2554` at **7**, and the rest
where they were. Two files reached **zero** defects: `TeamDataScreen.tsx` and
`PlayerFiveYearPlan.tsx`.

**The gate, armed.** A bound of zero is only a measurement if the reader can still see what it
forbids. Two things were done. The same reader was run over a **mirror** of the quarantine carrying
one draft that calls `useState` without importing it, one that reaches for `React` without binding
it, and one sound draft beside them: it must name the first two and leave the third alone. And a
live arm planted the missing `useState` import back into a real draft —
`.drafts/features/academy/AcademyReport.tsx` — and ran the gate: it exits **1** with the forbidden
family red, the backlog red and the unbound family red; the file is then restored and a SHA-256 of
its bytes before and after is identical. The control run is green.

**Honest reservation.** The quarantine's types are still not right, and this milestone does not claim
they are. **423** defects remain across **69** of the **79** drafts, and the biggest family of them
(`2322`, "not assignable", **280** of them) was not touched: telling a value from a type is a
question about what the code means, and no rule answers it. One family was deliberately left out of
the repair, and the reason is worth naming: **14** defects are names the app exports and the draft
never imports — `EmptyState` (**4**), `browserStore` (**2**), `useI18n` (**2**), and `readJson`,
`writeJson`, `calculateTransferFee`, `newsData`, `prev` and `syncedCount` (**1** each). Repairing
them means knowing which module exports each name, and deriving that means reading the app's module
graph — which is exactly the thing `proof-app-tree.mjs` pins the count of. A repair that hard-codes
the nine mappings would fix the pile and teach the next draft nothing; the honest next unit derives
the export index and reads it. Until then, the two families this milestone repaired are at **zero**,
every other family is bounded, and the backlog is a number that can only go down.

**One coupling worth naming.** The gaps block still carries **M538**: the concurrent line of work has
that number in flight, and by the ledger's own arithmetic a number between the oldest and the newest
heading with no section of its own is a gap until it lands one. The paragraph above the block named
the block's size in **words** — "one hundred and five" — while the block held **107**; the figure is
now carried as a numeral and read by `scripts/proof-ledger-run.mjs`, so a milestone that changes the
block without changing the sentence is refused.

### M537 — the thirteen that no rule could repair, repaired by hand

**What the gauge says.** `scripts/proof-drafts.mjs` **8/8** (the count is unchanged; one clause changed
and one was added). The quarantine holds **80** source drafts, and it now holds **0** that do not
parse, with **0** diagnostics between them. When this milestone began the same census read **13**
broken files and **102** diagnostics: **13** files were repaired by hand and **102** diagnostics left
the pile. The gate's registry was emptied and its two ceilings were lowered from 13 and 102 to **0**
and **0** in the same landing, so the ratchet now holds the pile at nothing rather than at thirteen.

**Why they needed a hand.** The thirteen M536 left behind were not families. Each was one author's
one mistake, and each had to be read as a question — what did this line mean to say? — before it
could be answered. A rule can repair "a `t("key)` whose closing quote is missing", because the shape
is the same everywhere and the repair cannot change what the author meant. A rule cannot repair "the
date literal says `` `${currentYear}-08-12", time": "20:00" ``", because the answer depends on which
of the two adjacent quotes the author meant to close.

**The rule a hand-repair had to pass.** Three, and the repair script enforces all three rather than
the author honouring them:
1. the needle must match **exactly once** in the file — a repair that hit two places, or none, stops
   the run before a byte is written;
2. the file's line endings must not be mixed, and the file is written back in the endings it already
   had, so the write cannot silently re-encode a file the ledger counts in bytes;
3. after the repair, the same TypeScript parser that reads the pile must report **zero** diagnostics
   for that file — not fewer. A repair that left a file still broken did not land at all.

**The thirteen, and what each one was.** **28** patches over **13** files, and the **102** diagnostics
they removed by kind: a stray quote inside a union type (`"buy"" | "sell"`) and a parenthesis that
closed a `useMemo(` call before the block it opened, both in `ManagerAgent.tsx` (**9**); a
Python-style conditional in a JavaScript expression, answered with the ternary the author was
reaching for, in `CoachStatistics.tsx` (**4**); a plugin list held in a `useMemo` whose body the
author had emptied with a `/* toggle plugin */` comment, answered by making the list state and the
comment a real `togglePlugin` handler, in `AdvancedPluginSystem.tsx` (**1**); a ternary whose false
branch lost its closing quote, in `DataSync.tsx` (**3**); a `t()` call closed by `}%` where the
author meant `%)}`, in `SalaryCapAnalysis.tsx` (**1**); a self-closing element that was never closed,
in `SeasonOps.tsx` (**1**); a `</div>` where the element the author opened was a `</Panel>`, in
`SeasonReport.tsx` (**1**); two `t()` interpolations never closed and three doubled braces
(`{{p.name}[0]}`, `{{p.name}}`, `{{p.overall}}`) where the author meant one, in `SquadDepth.tsx`
(**5**); three date literals that lost the quote closing the template and the one opening the time,
plus three template literals never closed, in `SeasonSchedule.tsx` (**30**); a template literal never
closed, in `MediaLibrary.tsx` (**13**); a conditional never closed and a `.map(…)` whose own
container was closed by a `</div>`, in `NewsArchiveAdvanced.tsx` (**8**); and a Rust-style `switch`
expression answered with the descending ternary chain its arms describe, in `ContractPrediction.tsx`
(**13**) and `PlayerContractDetails.tsx` (**13**).

**A partial repair can make a file worse.** `SeasonSchedule.tsx` is the proof, and it is worth
keeping because the rule that caught it is the rule this milestone rests on. The first repair removed
the stray quotes from the three date literals and changed nothing else: the file's diagnostics went
from **30** to **36**. Closing the three date templates — the real defect, and the one the stray
quotes were masking — but leaving the other three templates open took it to **33**. Only the
complete repair reaches **0**. A gate that accepted "fewer diagnostics" would have accepted a file
that got worse twice; this one accepts only zero, and it is the same parser that reads the pile
every time the gate runs.

**A rendering that is not byte-accurate.** The stray `)` in `ManagerAgent.tsx` was invisible in the
rendering this session read the file through: the line appeared as `}> = [];` where the bytes held
`}> = []);`. That `)` closed the `useMemo(` call before the block it opened, which is why the parser
complained about the `;` several lines later and not about the `)`. Six minimal reproductions were
written to test whether the type annotation was itself illegal — it is not, in TSX or in TS. The
needle rule is what caught it: every repair is matched against raw bytes and must match exactly
once, so a rendering that cannot be trusted never reaches the file.

**The gate, armed.** The registry is empty, and a belt that scrapes nothing is green for the wrong
reason, so two things were done. The rule the registry encodes — a draft that now parses comes off
the list, a new broken draft goes on it — was folded into a single clause that reads the pile and
the registry in both directions. And the census was made to run over a **mirror** of the quarantine
with one broken draft planted in it and one sound draft beside it: the reader must name the first
and leave the second alone. The arm confirms that a breach would be caught: with a syntax defect
planted in one draft, the gate exits **1** with both the registry clause and the ceiling clause
red, and the tree is byte-identical afterwards (a SHA-256 of the file before and after).

**Honest reservation.** This milestone made thirteen files parse. It did not make them correct, and
it does not claim to: a draft that parses may still import a module that is itself quarantined, miss
a type, read a `t()` key no locale carries, or interpolate a value into a `className` that no
attribute ever reads. The layer beneath syntax is untouched, and it is the next thing the pile needs
— a census that reads the drafts the way this one does, but asks what the types say rather than
whether the tokens parse. Until that census exists, the honest statement is that the quarantine's
**syntax** backlog is closed and nothing else about it is.

**One coupling worth naming.** The gaps block still carries **M534**: the concurrent line of work
has that number in flight, and by the ledger's own arithmetic a number between the oldest and the
newest heading with no section of its own is a gap until it lands one.

### M536 — the quarantine's parse backlog, repaired family by family

**What the gauge says.** `scripts/proof-drafts.mjs` **8/8** (unchanged). The quarantine holds **80**
source drafts, and it now holds **13** that do not parse, with **102** diagnostics between them. When
this milestone began the same census read **50** broken files and **841** diagnostics: **37** files
were repaired outright, **49** files changed, and **739** diagnostics left the pile. The gate's
ceilings were lowered from 50 and 841 to 13 and 102 in the same landing, so the ratchet holds the
pile where it now stands rather than where it stood.

**Six families, and what each was worth.** The pile was not one mistake but six repeatable ones, and
each was repaired by a rule that the parser then had to agree with. A bare template used as an
attribute value — 88 occurrences in 32 files, worth **187** diagnostics. A bare expression used as an
attribute value — 94 occurrences in 35 files, worth **340**. A `t("key)` whose closing quote was
missing — 49 occurrences in 15 files, worth **125**. A `.map(…)` whose JSX container was closed by
`))` and never by `}` — 23 occurrences in 19 files, worth **23**. An interpolation inside a
double-quoted attribute — 7 occurrences in 6 files, worth **60**. And the `)` the parser itself
named, inserted at the offset the parser named — worth **4**.

**The rule a repair had to pass.** No change was kept on the strength of a pattern matching. The
same TypeScript parser that reads the pile had to read strictly fewer diagnostics for that file
after the change, and no repair was allowed to remove a token that was there before it. The
expression family additionally had to sit inside an opening tag — a JSX attribute, not an assignment
in a script body. Both guards carry their own self-test, armed at the top of the repair script and
checked before any file is touched: a tag case that must be caught and a tag case that must not be,
a token case that must be refused and a token case that must pass.

**A bug the guards did not catch, and why the third one exists.** The `t("key)` family was written
wrong first: the replacement dropped the `t` and left `("key")`. The file still parsed, and the
diagnostic count still fell, so the diagnostic rule and the tag rule both passed it — a wrong repair
that the measurements approved. A human read of the diff caught it. The token rule was written next,
and it is the rule that would have refused that change. It refuses nothing in the landed run,
because the family was fixed before the run, and its self-test still refuses the shape that slipped
through.

**A scanner bug worth naming too.** The interpolation family was applied by a scanner that
understands strings and templates, not by a line regex. Its first version began looking for the
attribute's closing quote from inside the interpolation, so it matched the `"` of a ternary's own
string literals (`type === "shareRate"`) and stopped there. That version left 30 broken files and
157 diagnostics on the tree. Beginning the search just after the interpolation brought it to 13 and
102.

**What is still broken, and why it was left.** The thirteen that remain are not mechanical. A stray
quote in a union type, a Python-style conditional, an arrow whose body is only a comment, an
unterminated string in a ternary, a `}%` where the author meant `%)}`, two mismatched closing tags, a
doubled brace inside an interpolation, a mangled date literal, an unterminated template literal, a
fragment with no parent element, and two Rust-style `switch` expressions. Each asks what the author
meant, and a parser cannot answer that. They are named in the gate's registry, they are counted by
the ceiling, and they wait for a milestone that can read the screens.

**Honest reservation.** The repair was mechanical, and mechanical is all it was: it made files
parse, it did not make them correct. A draft that parses may still import a module that is itself
quarantined, miss a type, or read a `t()` key no locale carries — parse-clean is not shippable, and
this milestone does not claim otherwise. Where a repair had to guess — wrapping a bare attribute
value in braces is a guess about what the author meant — the guess is visible in the diff, and the
file is a draft behind a dot prefix, not a screen anyone sees.

**One coupling worth naming.** The gaps block still carries **M534**: the concurrent line of work
has that number in flight, and by the ledger's own arithmetic a number between the oldest and the
newest heading with no section of its own is a gap until it lands one.

### M535 — the parse backlog is measured, and the ten cheapest drafts are repaired

**What the gauge says.** `scripts/proof-drafts.mjs` **8/8** (it was 5/5). The quarantine holds **80**
source drafts; **50** of them do not parse, with **841** diagnostics between them. When this
milestone measured it, the same census read **60** broken files and **861** diagnostics. Ten files
were repaired in the same landing, taking **20** diagnostics out of the pile.

**Why a gate.** M522 moved the lane's unshipped batch behind a dot prefix so the app's census would
read the app again, and M525 charged the boundary in both directions. Neither said anything about the
quarantine itself: how much of the pile parses was a number only a person could recompute by hand, and
by hand it rots. The new clause measures the pile with the TypeScript parser, names every file in it,
and holds the totals where they are. A draft that starts parsing has to come off the list, a new
broken draft has to go on it, and the counts are bounded at **50** files and **841** diagnostics.

**The claim is narrow on purpose, and the narrowness is the point.** It is about SYNTAX. A draft that
parses may still import a module that is itself quarantined, miss a type, or read a `t()` key no
locale carries — parse-clean is not shippable. What the clause buys is that the syntactic backlog
cannot quietly grow, and that the ledger says which files are in it.

**What was repaired.** Five screens were a missing `}` after a `.map(...)` expression; four used a
backtick template where JSX wants an expression container; `ClubFinance` held two sibling grids in
one JSX expression, which is now a fragment; and `TacticalDashboard`'s success rate had a ternary
with a `?` and no `:` — the author's intent, a percentage over zero tackles, is written out. The
quarantined backup tool was CommonJS in a `.mjs`: it is written as ESM now, and the `backups/`
directory it used to create on import is created when a backup is taken instead. The tool was run in a
scratch directory: it parses, it backs up, and it exports its four functions.

**Armed both ways.** The reader is exercised on a fixture first — a broken snippet is seen and a sound
one is not — and each of the three new clauses was then flipped red on its own and the bytes
restored: a new broken draft read **1 unnamed** and **51 broken**; a registered draft rewritten to
parse read **1 stale**; a registered draft broken further read **843 diagnostics**. All three came
back to **8/8**.

**Honest reservation.** The list is a ledger the lane's resurrections will keep touching. A draft
that leaves `.drafts/` is CLOSED — reported, not charged — so a resurrection cannot redden a gate
about syntax; a draft repaired in place has to be taken off the list, or the gate says so. The
ceilings are a bound rather than a pin: they are lowered as the pile shrinks, and a ceiling with
slack above it is slack, not a lie. Nothing here claims the fifty remaining drafts are fit to ship;
ten of them are now closer to it.

**One coupling worth naming.** The gaps block now carries **M534**: the concurrent line of work has
that number in flight, and by the ledger's own arithmetic a number between the oldest and the newest
heading with no section of its own is a gap until it lands one. If that unit lands with a section of
its own, the entry comes off the list — the ledger's rule, not a favour.

### M534 — the run-in: what every club still has to face, weighed by the clubs it faces

**What the gauge says.** `proof-i18n` **383/383**, `proof-screens` **31/31**, `proof-app-tree`
**12/12**, `proof-coverage` **26/26**, `proof-storage` **61/61**, `proof-analytics` **80/80**,
`proof-last` **10/10**, `tsc --noEmit` clean, `npm run build` exit 0, bundle **496 → 499 KB**
gzip, recorded.

**Why not the fixture forecast.** The Data Room already prints the next four scheduled fixtures
of a competition through `fixtureForecast`, and every scheduled row in Football World carries its
match probability. A board of the same numbers would be the app's second copy of one read. What
no screen answered is the aggregate question a manager actually asks in April: **for each club,
how hard is what is left?**

**The unit of difficulty.** `domain/analytics.ts` grows `runIn(compId, matches, clubs)` — for
every club, the opponents still on its calendar (this competition's `SCHEDULED` fixtures, in
kickoff order) and the average points-per-game of those opponents, two decimals. Rows come back
hardest first, and a club with nothing left keeps zero and sits last, so an empty calendar can
never be mistaken for the easiest run-in. Each row also carries the club's own record, because
"tough run-in" means nothing without "for whom".

**What it does.** Competition chips, four tiles (toughest run-in, easiest run-in, fixtures left,
and the league average of what remains), then the board: crest, name and record, fixtures left,
opponent PPG against a bar scaled to the hardest, and the short names of the clubs still to
play. A competition with no fixtures left says so rather than drawing an empty chart. Route
`/run-in`, a sidebar entry, and eighteen keys — `nav.runIn` plus seventeen `runIn.*` — across
en / zh-CN / zh-TW.

**The doors it had to use.** `runIn` and its `teamMetrics` / `byKickoff` ordering in the domain;
`sum` for the totals; `last` (the last-element door) for the easiest row instead of an inline
`xs[xs.length - 1]`; `ABSENT` wherever a figure or a club name is missing; `fmt2` for the
two-decimal averages; `pctOf` for the bar width.

**The pins paid.** `APP_SRC_PIN` 117→118, `TSX_PIN` 61→62, `SRC_PIN` 120→121, literal `t()`
sites 1486→1506, placeholder sites 156→160, duplicate-value / excess-key counts 126→127 and
214→215; `APP_MODULE_PIN` 112→113 in `proof-app-tree`; `POP_PIN` 112→113, `BY_DIR_PIN.features`
38→39 and `DEEP_PIN` 54→55 in `proof-coverage`; `APP_FILES_PIN` 107→108 in `proof-storage`;
`proof-last`'s reader list plus one reader; `proof-fmt2`'s consumer list plus one file;
`proof-absent-glyph`'s user ledger plus one file and five cells; `proof-absent-name`'s carrier
set plus one file and three sites.

**Honest reservation.** The difficulty is today's table, not a forecast: a club's run-in looks
hard because the clubs left on it have earned points so far, and the remaining matches can
change exactly that. The average is unweighted — a single postponed giant counts as much as
three mid-table sides. And on a finished competition every row reads zero; the screen shows the
empty state there rather than pretending a number exists.

### M533 — projecting any player: the growth model as a scouting read

**What the gauge says.** `proof-i18n` **383/383**, `proof-screens` **31/31**, `proof-app-tree`
**12/12**, `proof-coverage` **26/26**, `proof-storage` **61/61**, `tsc --noEmit` clean, `npm run
build` exit 0, bundle **494 → 496 KB** gzip, recorded.

**The same model, a different subject.** `projectGrowth` already replays the training loop's
diminishing-returns per-session gain, but it was only ever pointed at the *reader's own* profile on
the Development screen. This unit points it at **any** of the six hundred and ten players: pick a
player, pick weeks / sessions-per-week / session rating, and the focus is the three **weakest**
attributes (`weakestAttributes`) — the honest "if they keep working on their gaps, where do they
land?" a scout asks before a bid. The potential ceiling (`attrCeiling`) is shown beside the
projection so the reader can see the headroom the model is aiming inside.

**What it does.** A player picker (all players, strongest first), three cadence selectors, the
player's club / position / age / potential, and a projected table — each focus attribute's now →
projected value and delta, then the overall before → after. Route `/projection`, a sidebar entry,
sixteen keys across en / zh-CN / zh-TW.

**The doors it had to use.** `projectGrowth` for the model, `weakestAttributes` for the focus,
`attrCeiling` for the ceiling, `byOverall` for the picker order — and the attribute names resolve
through `t(\`attr.name.${key}\`)`, the same dynamic site the Development screen uses, which meant
declaring the new site in `proof-i18n`'s dynamic table rather than spelling a second label lane.

**The pins paid.** `APP_SRC_PIN` 116→117, `TSX_PIN` 60→61, `SRC_PIN` 119→120, literal sites
1467→1486 and the template count 108→109, plus the duplicate-value / excess-key counts 125→126 and
210→214 in `proof-i18n` (and one new dynamic-site row); `APP_MODULE_PIN` 111→112 in
`proof-app-tree`; `POP_PIN` 111→112, `BY_DIR_PIN.features` 37→38 and `DEEP_PIN` 53→54 in
`proof-coverage`; `APP_FILES_PIN` 106→107 in `proof-storage`.

**Honest reservation.** The projection trains the three weakest traits by default; a player whose
ceiling is already reached will barely move, which is correct but can look like a broken screen
until the reader sees the potential beside it. And like every model here it is deterministic and
transparent — it is not a prediction of what a real player will become.

### M532 — the league's leaders, folded from the fixtures themselves

**What the gauge says.** `proof-i18n` **383/383**, `proof-screens` **31/31**, `proof-app-tree`
**12/12**, `proof-coverage` **26/26**, `proof-storage` **61/61**, `tsc --noEmit` clean, `npm run
build` exit 0, bundle **493 → 494 KB** gzip, recorded.

**A board that is a fold, not a table.** Every goal and card in the seeded fixtures is already a
`MatchEvent` on the match record — 948 goals, 434 yellows and 108 reds across 1,566 fixtures — so the
leaderboard is computed by walking those events, never stored. The key is `clubId|playerName`, which
keeps two same-named players on different clubs apart, and the club comes from the event's own side
of the fixture rather than a name lookup. Read once in a `useMemo`; a stored table could drift from
the fixtures it summarises, a fold cannot.

**What it does.** Two boards: the **top fifteen scorers** (goals, with club and position) and the
**ten most-booked** players (yellow and red counts), each ranked with ties broken by name. Route
`/leaders`, a sidebar entry, nine keys across en / zh-CN / zh-TW.

**The pins paid.** `APP_SRC_PIN` 115→116, `TSX_PIN` 59→60, `SRC_PIN` 118→119 and literal sites
1457→1467 in `proof-i18n`; `APP_MODULE_PIN` 110→111 in `proof-app-tree`; `POP_PIN` 110→111,
`BY_DIR_PIN.features` 36→37 and `DEEP_PIN` 52→53 in `proof-coverage`; `APP_FILES_PIN` 105→106 in
`proof-storage`.

**Honest reservation.** The board counts the seeded dataset's fixtures, and it groups by player
*name* (the events carry a name, not an id), so two identically named players in the same club would
merge — the `clubId|name` key removes the cross-club case but not the same-club one. It also reads
only finished fixtures that carry events (1,064 of 1,566); the rest contribute no goals, which is
correct but means the totals are a subset of the season.

### M525 — the drafts are one-way, and the boundary is a gate

**What the gauge says.** `scripts/proof-drafts.mjs` **5/5**. The app is **104** modules in ten
directories and the drafts hold **59** files; the scan reads **241** files and **1253** specifiers
across the app, the tests and the tooling, and finds **0** crossings into `.drafts`.

**Why a gate.** M522 moved the lane's unshipped batch behind a dot prefix, and the shared rule
(`scripts/lib/appTree.mjs`) is what makes it invisible: every census skips a hidden name. But only
one half of that was charged. Nothing said a *shipped* file may not import across the boundary —
`from "../../.drafts/features/coach/CoachProfile"` would put a draft back in the module graph while
every number in this ledger still read the old population. So the gate asks five questions: the rule
names `.drafts` hidden and an ordinary directory not; a planted module inside the quarantine stays
out of the walk while its sibling counts; no source imports anything that resolves inside `.drafts`
(relative and `@/` alias, static, dynamic and `require`); every draft sits at `.drafts/<its original
path>`; and the drafts README still carries the two mechanisms a resurrector must honour — `git mv`
and `@source not "../.drafts"`.

**Armed both ways.** The reader is exercised on a fixture: three crossing shapes are charged and a
sibling, a bare package and an import-shaped string are not. Each clause was then flipped red on its
own and the bytes restored: a dead `import()` of a draft inside the gate itself read **1 crossing**;
a loose file at the top of `.drafts` read **malformed 1**; dropping `git mv` from the README read
**git mv false**. All three came back to **5/5**.

**Where it landed.** The gate was written for this milestone, but a concurrent commit swept it out
of the working tree before this section existed — an `add` of the shared index took the untracked
file — so it is already in M524's commit. This landing is its record: the five clauses, the three
arms, and the two comment lines that same sweep left in `proof-app-tree.mjs` claiming a list entry
that was never there, removed here.

**Honest reservation.** A live copy of a drafted path is printed, not charged: that is a
resurrection in progress, and the `git mv` that finishes it removes the draft (M524's coach résumé
was the first, and the drafts fell from 61 to 59). The scan is JS/TS only — a stylesheet cannot
import across the boundary, and Tailwind is told not to read the directory at all.

**The rapid lane's batch follows it in (M526–M553).** A concurrent line of work shipped thirty new
screens straight into `features/` — academy, coach, community, core, injury, match, media, player,
scout, tactical, transfer — and every one was unshipped: reachable from nothing in `App.tsx`'s route
graph. They broke the census the way M522's batch did (the i18n walk read **139** modules against a
pin of **109** and **446** `t()` calls named keys no dictionary held), so this unit moves all thirty
behind the dot prefix with `git mv`, each preserved at `.drafts/<its original path>`; four already
had an older draft and the newer copy replaces it. Out of the walk, the i18n gate reads **383/383**
again and the module count returns to its pin. The season report — M525's own deliverable — lands
with it: `domain/worldEngine.ts` derives a whole-run report (per-season rows, dynasties, the biggest
rise and fall, whole-run market and rating growth) from the snapshot the engine already reproduces
deterministically, `DynamicWorld` renders it, and the bundle grows **475 → 482 KB** gzip, recorded in
`tests/perf/baseline.json` as a decision rather than a drift. `npm run proof` **118/118 scripts**.

### M500 — the twelfth direction: an option no caller ever reaches

**What the gauge says.** `scripts/proof-param-options.mjs` **5/5**. The shipped tree declares
**35** options across **34** top-level functions and a caller reaches every one (**0** unreached),
read on both planes: **160** project modules and **89** typed calls into those functions, plus
**124** proof scripts whose `vite.ssrLoadModule` bindings map back to **404** exported names and
**212** calls. Before the fold the same census charged **3** of **38** options over **37**
functions: `scoutReport.top`, `modelPlayerProfile.top` and `useFilmRecords.rev`.

**The measurement came first.** M461 closed the props surface; its positional sibling was measured
before it was graded. Optional and defaulted parameters in top-level functions came to 37 functions
and 38 options, of which three were unreached — every one exported and read, so a scan that only
asked whether the parameter's body reads it would have called all three alive. Two nearby surfaces
were measured and dropped for lack of a unit: exported record interfaces and the bundled assets,
each with no unread member to fold.

**The reader.** An option is reached when any resolved call site passes an argument at that index.
The typed plane follows import aliases, namespace-qualified callees, `.call` (the receiver is
sliced off) and `.apply` (arity unknown). The scripts are plain JS whose values are `any`, so
syntactic arity is their evidence: `const { a: b } = await server.ssrLoadModule(...)`,
destructuring from a loaded namespace variable, and `NS.fn(...)` all map back to the exported name.
Five shapes cannot be attributed and are read whole: a function with no call site; a function used
as a value (a callback argument, an object-carried reference such as `{ Fx }` or `holder.Fx`); any
spread argument; a script binding used outside a call; and, in the typed plane, the receiver of a
method call, which is a call site rather than a value (`FxCall.call(...)`). A green may never rest
on an unattributable call, so the tree clause prints the clamped buckets instead of folding them
into a zero: today **3** functions have no call site (`lazyLoadCSS`, `useTouchThrottle`,
`useTouchDetection`), **1** is value-referenced (`englishWord`), **0** spreads, and **3** script
bindings are clamped (`weakestAttributes`, `englishWord`, `formatDate`).

**Three folds, one reason.** `scoutReport(p, top = 5)` and `modelPlayerProfile(p, top = 6)` each
passed `top` into one slice or one `strongestAttributes` call, and no shipped caller ever passed a
second argument; both are constants at their use now, 5 and 6, so every number the screens already
displayed is unchanged. `useFilmRecords(rev = 0)` fed its argument only to a `useMemo` dependency
list and no caller passed it; its sibling `useFilmClips(rev)` keeps `rev` and is called with one at
`ReviewPage.tsx`, so this was a per-function measurement rather than a family-wide cleanup.

**The seam, charged both ways.** Thirteen arms, **13/13 matched, 0 interfered**. One drops an
argument at a fixture caller and asserts the charge; eight break the reader one joint at a time
(typed arity, script arity, spread, the `.call` receiver slice, the no-call clamp, the
value-reference clamp, the script-value clamp and the script-clamp disclosure); one unmaps script
bindings and loses the binding floor; one stops mapping namespace destructuring and reds the tree
clause and that floor; one reverts the typed-call floor; one is a comment-only control. The first
pass mispredicted four, and one was a real fixture weakness: both value-referenced fixture
functions were also uncalled, so removing the value-reference clamp charged nothing. The fixture
now calls one of them with fewer arguments than its option and the arm reds. The other three
predictions mis-attributed consequences — unmapping script bindings also unmarks a script spread,
namespace destructuring supplies more than two hundred bindings, and the typed plane already
reaches every function the script-value clamp was guarding. A fifth misprediction came from the
rebase: the no-call clamp is what keeps the three exported functions the lane landed without a
call site out of the charge, so removing it reds the real-tree clause as well as the fixture's
charge — [1,3] rather than [1].

**What the gauge says about the suite.** `npx tsc --noEmit` exit 0, `npm run build` exit 0,
`npm run proof` **82/117 scripts (3052/3154 checks)** — and this unit's gate is green inside that
run (`proof:param-options` **5/5**). The **35** red scripts are the concurrent lane's code-only
batch, not this unit's edit: `proof-dead-exports` charges **65** dead exports (the academy,
coach, league and manager screens, `domain/finance.ts`), `proof-dead-imports` **146** dead
bindings, `proof-coverage` **66** of **167** app modules unreachable from `src/main.tsx` with a

**Honest reservation.** The population is top-level function declarations and `const` function
initialisers, so a defaulted parameter on a class or object method is outside it. A call made
through `Function.prototype.bind` is not resolved: the tree's fifteen `.bind` uses are all on
compiler hosts or `localStorage`, none on a charged function, but unlike `.call`/`.apply` the
shape is not pinned, so a future bound call would charge its options as unreached rather than
clamp. And script evidence is syntactic by nature — a spread is refused (arity unknown) and a
binding invoked rather than called is clamped, but a script cannot make a runtime-computed arity
visible.

**The number, and what the lane did to it.** A concurrent lane ships one screen or script per
commit and never writes a section. Its first batch reused the labels M461 and M462 — my previous

### M458 — the app installs, the shell survives offline, and the budget is measured

PLAN-LONGTERM.md's M458: installable, offline-cached, and honest about what a first paint costs. The shell is four files — `public/manifest.webmanifest` (standalone, `#05070a`, an SVG icon that is also maskable), `public/icon.svg`, `public/sw.js` and the links in `index.html` — and `src/main.tsx` registers the worker **behind `import.meta.env.PROD`**, because a worker in dev caches the module graph and turns every edit into a hard reload.

**The worker's rules, in the order they apply.** Same-origin GET only; the API (`/functions/`) is never cached, because a stale API answer is a lie about the world; navigations are network-first with a cached-shell fallback, so an offline deep link still opens the app; static assets are stale-while-revalidate, so a cached asset paints immediately and refreshes behind the scene. The cache name carries a version and `activate` drops every other cache. There is deliberately **no precache list**: the build is hash-named, so a list would be stale the moment the build changes — runtime caching with a versioned name is the strategy that cannot lie about its contents.

**The budget, measured not promised.** The plan's "3G first paint" has no browser to measure it yet, so the proof measures what ships: 475 KB gzip across 34 assets (JS 463, CSS 12.5), pinned at 520 KB. When M459's E2E suite lands it can replace the proxy with a real throttled measurement; until then the number is at least taken from the real build with zlib, not from the source's intentions.

**The seam, charged both ways.** `scripts/proof-pwa.mjs` (4/4) runs four pure predicates over the files — manifest completeness, the shell link, the production guard, the worker's ten rules — and each one is fed a broken fixture it must refuse (no `display`, no maskable icon, no manifest link, a dev-only registration, a worker without the API guard, without the origin guard, without the shell fallback). The bundle budget reads `dist/assets` and reddens when the pin is exceeded.

**A debt paid in passing.** The working tree carried 105 duplicated dictionary lines — the career keys M453 added, staged again on top of a HEAD that already had them (M454's commit had swept them in). The duplicate reddened `tsc` with 105 TS1117s, and this unit restores the dictionary to HEAD and rebuilds green. The lesson is M453's own: a commit's pathspec is a promise to the whole change, and a file left out of it does not stay put — it gets swept into somebody else's commit, or duplicated in a later one.

**The measurement came before the gate, and it moved the unit.** M456's closing paragraph named the
dictionary as the next surface. That census was measured first: `proof-i18n` already owns it —
check 16 requires every dynamic site to be declared and every declared site to be live, check 17

clean — ten actions and ten persisted slices, every one with a caller. The surface that did carry
debt is the declaration layer one step out: a record can be exported, constructed, and still offer
a field no screen, domain module or proof ever reads.

**The reader.** Declaration identity is the wrong join here. The engine's shape is mirrored into
`domain/types.ts` and the screens read the mirror — `SimTeamStats` is read through the structurally
identical `MatchStats` at `features/football/Details.tsx` — so an identity census charged **78** of

reader asks instead whether any access of the field's name lands on a value whose type is assignable
to the record, in either direction. An `any` receiver (a parsed document, an untyped seed) reads by
name, which is the conservative answer: it can miss a dead field, never invent one. Destructuring is
resolved through the declaration it binds — a variable initializer, a parameter, or a for-of element
— and string element access counts. Unlike a context's provider wiring, a model module reading its
own record is a real consumer, so reads inside the declaring file count.

the counter reading its own fixture is not a consumer, and counting it would make the population

### M456 — the ninth direction: a provider field no consumer reads

**What the gauge says.** `scripts/proof-context-readers.mjs` **5/5**. The app declares **4**
contexts — `I18nValue` in `i18n/index.tsx`, `RouterValue` in `lib/router.tsx`,
`ThemeContextValue` in `lib/theme.tsx` and `OsContext` in `store/useFootballOS.tsx` — and the
folded tree offers **20** fields, every one with a consumer outside its declaring file (**0**
unread). Before the fold the same census read **23** fields and charged **3**: `I18nValue.locales`,
`RouterValue.segments`, `ThemeContextValue.setTheme`. The program parses **100** shipped modules,
every context resolves to a same-file interface, and none is unresolved.

**The measurement came before the gate.** The store's surface — twelve actions and ten persisted
slices — was the first candidate, and every one already had a reader, so nothing was charged. A
per-declaration interface-member census was measured and rejected before it could ship: TypeScript
joins a read to a field by shape, not by declaration, so it charged live fields (`AiMemoryEntry.at`,
read through an unrelated local seed type) and went blind on dynamic element access
(`MEMORY_DETAIL[m.kind]`). The context surface is the same question asked where identity is
decidable: the field is reached through a hook whose return type is the interface.

**The reader.** A `createContext<T | null>` whose `T` is an interface declared in the same file. A
field is read when another file destructures it (`const { toggle } = useTheme()`), renames it
(`{ toggle: flip }`), reaches it through a member access (`useThing().member`) or a string element
access, and the resolved symbol's declaration is that interface member. Reads inside the declaring
file are the provider's own wiring, not consumers. A context whose type argument is not a same-file
interface is charged as unresolved, never skipped.

**What is NOT claimed.** Identity is the join, so a field reached only through a structurally equal
local type is charged even when a context value was assigned to it — the census never exempts. An
imported context type or an inline type literal is charged as unresolved rather than followed. A
bare `useContext(Context)` call is not resolved to a field (all four hooks here go through a named
`use*` function). The fixture pins these edges: a twin interface with the same field names reads
nothing, and a read in the provider's own file reads nothing.

**The fold.** Three fields left with their wiring: `setTheme` was a wrapper around the provider's
own `setThemeState` that no screen called (consumers read only `theme` and `toggle`), `segments` was
a derived split of `path` that no consumer read (they match routes against `path` with
`matchRoute`), and `locales` was a copy of `LOCALES` with no reader — `LOCALES` itself stays
exported, imported directly by the two language switchers and read by `detectLocale`. Three files,
no behaviour change.

**Two gates already pinned that surface.** `proof-storage.mjs` asserted that both theme mutators
were functions, and `proof-router.mjs` parsed a hash into `path / segments / query`. Both checks
described the published cap, so the fold updated them to the surface the screens read: the theme cap
publishes exactly `theme,toggle`, and the router's cap carries exactly `navigate,path,query`, with
the trailing-slash case reading `path` verbatim instead of a segment list. Neither file lost a
check; their assertions now name the smaller surface.

**The arms.** `dev/.m456-arms.mjs` runs **12/12** on the isolated plane, each arm restored
byte-exactly and the plane's `git status` compared to its baseline. Fixture arms: dropping the
destructuring read (A), adding a second unread field (B) and reading the ghost through member access
(J) each charge clause 1, while a field read only by its own provider stays charged (C, control);
dropping the broken fixture from the program silences the unresolved charge and reds clause 2 (K).
Real-tree arms: a dead field in `ThemeContextValue` (D), in `RouterValue` (E), and a rename that
leaves the old key unread (F) each charge clause 3; a context whose type is not a same-file
interface charges clause 4 (G); a new field with a consumer stays green (H) and a renamed
destructuring binding still reads its property (I, both controls); a skip set naming a field charges
clause 5 (L). Predicted from each clause's own sentence: A[1] B[1] C[] D[3] E[3] F[3] G[4] H[] I[]
J[1] K[2] L[5]. All twelve matched, and at rest and after every arm the plane's status equalled its
baseline.

**One fixture lesson.** The first fixture run read **0** of its four fields: the consumer's relative
import resolved to `any`, silently, because Bundler module resolution stats the fixture directory
and canonicalises the path before probing the file — the virtual host answered `fileExists` but not
`directoryExists` or `realpath`. The host now serves one canonical `SourceFile` per virtual path
and answers all three, and the fixture went from 0 reads to the 2 it should see. A fixture that
cannot resolve its own import is not a fixture: every field is charged, and the gate's red would
have been blamed on the reader.

**Next.** The dictionary is the next app-owned declaration surface: `i18n/dictionaries.ts` declares
thousands of rows, and a key no lookup reads is the same debt one layer over. Dynamic lookups are
real (`attr.name.${code}`, `group.${code}`, `prof.mode.${code}`, `dna.arch.${code}`), so the reader
has to expand a template's values from the list that enumerates them before any key is charged.
That census is measured before anything is charged.

`tsc --noEmit` exit 0, `npm run build` exit 0, and the full suite is green (113/113 proof scripts proven, 3134/3134 checks counted).

selectors `.dark`, `.fo-rise`, `.fo-live-dot`), **2** keyframes are read through an `animation`
value (`fo-rise`, `fo-pulse`), and **0** through neither. The one sheet is balanced, every at-rule
block parses (7), and the walk covers **287** code files.

**The measurement came before the gate.** A name-by-name grep of the unfolded sheet found exactly
two names that appear nowhere but their own declaration: `@utility scrollbar-gutter-stable` and
`@keyframes fo-shimmer`. An earlier reading had also named `fo-glass`, and that reading was wrong —
`fo-glass` is read as a conditional literal in `ui/primitives.tsx` (`glow && "fo-glass"`), which is
why the grep was corrected before anything was charged. The fold removed **2** declarations,
leaving 10 declared and 0 unread.

**The reader.** Three declaration kinds, two reader axes. An `@utility <x>` block and an `.x`
selector are read where the class token `x` appears in code — a `className` string, a `class`
attribute or an `@apply` — including variants (`hover:`), opacity (`/70`) and important suffixes. A
`@keyframes <x>` block is read by an `animation` / `animation-name` value in CSS or in an inline
style string, or by a `@theme --animate-*` value, which is how Tailwind 4 wires that namespace. An
at-rule header is not a reader of the declaration it introduces, a selector is not a reader of
itself, a comment reads nothing, and a selector-shaped string (`".foo"`) is not a class token. The
vendor stylesheet is skipped as in M432/M451/M454.

**What is NOT claimed.** The census reads spellings, not Tailwind's compiler: a class built at
runtime (`fo-${x}`) would not be seen, so a declaration read only that way would be charged.
Measured: no such construction exists in the tree today (no `bg-${…}`, `fo-${…}` or
`scrollbar-${…}` pattern). An inline-style `animation` string is read by its identifiers, not by a
browser, and a name that appears only in a keyframes header is still charged. Parse health is part
of the claim: every at-rule block must close and every sheet must balance, and a broken fixture
proves the check can see damage.

**The arms.** `dev/.m455-arms.mjs` runs **10/10** on the isolated plane, each arm restored
byte-exactly and the plane's `git status` compared to its baseline. Three fixture readers — a class
for a fixture utility (A), an animation value for a fixture keyframe (B) and a class attribute for a
fixture class selector (C) — each charge clause 1; a dead `@utility` (D), a dead `@keyframes` (E)
and a dead class selector (F) enter the real sheet and charge clause 2; an unbalanced sheet charges

green (H), a new keyframe read through an animation value stays green (I), and a selector-shaped
string does not read a class selector (J). Predicted from each clause's own sentence: A[1] B[1] C[1]
D[2] E[2] F[2] G[3] H[] I[] J[]. All ten matched, and at rest and after every arm the plane's
status equalled its baseline.

**One fixture lesson.** The first fixture run charged `keyframes fixture-motion` even though its
sample carried `"animation: fixture-motion 1s"`: the value reader's boundary set required
whitespace, `;` or `{` before `animation`, so an inline style string — where the quote is the
preceding character — was invisible. The fixture caught the gate's blind spot before the real tree
could hide a live keyframe behind it, and the set now includes the quote.

**Next.** The sheet's own declarations are all read now, so the next direction leaves the

### M454 — the seventh direction: a theme token no reader can see

**What the gauge says.** `scripts/proof-theme-tokens.mjs` **4/4**. `src/globals.css` declares
**66** custom properties — **31** in `:root`/`.dark` and **35** in `@theme inline` — and the census
finds a reader for every one: **43** are read through `var()`, **33** through a Tailwind utility
class, and **0** through neither. The three theme blocks are found, the one stylesheet is balanced,
every `@theme` namespace is modelled, and the walk covers **286** code files. No token is unread.

**The measurement came before the gate, and the first reading was wrong.** A probe over the
unfolded sheet declared **76** properties and found **zero** class readers — because its class
pattern asked for a literal hyphen before the stem (` -bg-card`), so no real class could match.
Fixed to read the stem itself, the same probe found **33** tokens read by class and **five** with
no reader at all: `--color-chart-1`, `--color-chart-2`, `--color-chart-5`,
`--color-sidebar-accent-foreground`, `--color-sidebar-ring`. Grep confirmed each name appears only
in its own declaration. The fold removed **15** declarations — the five `@theme` aliases and the
five `:root`/`.dark` pairs behind them — leaving 66 declared and 0 unread.

**The reader.** Two axes, because a theme token has two ways to be read. `var(--x)` is read
anywhere in code; the class axis derives the utility families Tailwind 4 generates from a
`@theme` namespace (`--color-*` → `bg-*`, `text-*`, `border-*`, …; `--radius-*` → `rounded-*`;
`--font-*` → `font-*`) and looks for the literal class, including variants (`hover:`), opacity
(`/80`) and important suffixes. A comment is not a reader; a longer class that merely starts with
the stem (`bg-ghostly` for `bg-ghost`) is not one either. A `@theme` namespace the gate does not
model is **refused**, not guessed, so a token whose reader the census cannot derive is never
charged. Parse health is part of the claim: the three blocks must be found and the braces balanced,
and a broken fixture proves the check can see damage.

**What is NOT claimed.** The census reads spellings, not Tailwind's compiler: a class built at
runtime (`bg-${tone}`) would not be seen, so a token read only by such a class would be charged.
Measured: no such construction exists in the tree today (no `bg-${…}`, `fo-${…}` or
`scrollbar-${…}` pattern), and the fixture's literal-class arms are the gate's own proof that the
axis can fire. The vendor stylesheet is skipped as in M432/M451, so its own declarations are not in
the population. `.dark` overrides are declarations; a token is read only if some code uses it.
The root colours are read where their `@theme` aliases call `var()`, and the gate does not
double-charge that path.

**The arms.** `dev/.m454-arms.mjs` runs **10/10** on the isolated plane, each arm restored
byte-exactly and the plane's `git status` compared to its baseline. A fixture class reader (A), a
fixture var reader (B) and a fixture ghost token (C) each charge clause 1; a dead theme token
enters the real sheet (D) and the sole class reader of a real token is renamed away (E) charge
clause 2; an unbalanced sheet (F) and an unmodelled namespace (G) charge clause 3. Three controls
separate the axes: a new token with a variant/opacity class stays green (H), a longer class that
only starts with the stem is charged (I), and a new token read through `var()` stays green (J).
Predicted from each clause's own sentence: A[1] B[1] C[1] D[2] E[2] F[3] G[3] H[] I[] J[]. All ten
matched, and at rest and after every arm the plane's status equalled its baseline.

**A lane straggler, and the base it landed on.** Rebasing onto the lane's three commits put this
unit on a tree whose suite was red in eight scripts, none of them this unit's own. One was this gate
reading a plane where the lane's committed `dev/` records had not checked out (restored, and the
